NEW YORK (CNN) — The husband of a woman whom authorities say was impaired by marijuana and alcohol when she caused a head-on collision that killed eight people, including herself, has rejected allegations that his wife abused substances.

Daniel Schuler, left, and his attorney, Dominic Barbara, spoke at a news conference Thursday.

“I’ve never seen her drunk since the day I met her,” Daniel Schuler said Thursday, referring to his wife, Diane. “I’m not angry at her. I’d marry her again tomorrow.”

Accompanied by his attorney, Schuler held the news conference to dispute statements by authorities, who said Tuesday that Diane Schuler, 36, had a blood alcohol level of 0.19 percent—more than twice the legal limit for drivers—and had marijuana in her system when she drove a minivan the wrong way on the Taconic State Parkway and collided head-on with an SUV.

Three adults in the SUV were killed in the July 26 crash, as were Schuler and four children—her daughter and three nieces—who were riding in the minivan. A fifth child in the minivan, Schuler’s son, survived.

On Thursday, Dominic Barbara, Daniel Schuler’s attorney, cited a list of medical ailments affecting Diane Schuler before the crash. She apparently had suffered from a tooth abscess for two months, had diabetes at “various levels,” and had a mysterious lump on her leg that seemed to move, he said.

“I think she had a stroke,” Barbara said, while acknowledging that he had no evidence to support the claim. “And I think from the stroke came all the other issues of what happened.”

The crash occurred about 30 miles north of New York City after Schuler and the children left a campground where her family had been staying. Barbara said no one at the campground saw Diane Schuler with alcohol. He said investigators interviewed nine people who spoke with her before she departed, and those individuals did not smell marijuana or alcohol on her breath.

“Actually, it was the opposite,” Barbara said. “She was happy. She was talking to people.”

Authorities said Tuesday that a broken vodka bottle was found in the minivan after the crash. Barbara said he could not explain the bottle but added, “Something had to have happened.”

Daniel Schuler and his attorney said they had not yet decided whether to seek another autopsy.

Jay Schuler, Daniel Schuler’s sister, said Thursday that Diane Schuler was reliable and loved children.

“There’s no way she’d do this,” Jay Schuler said. “She was responsible.”

The statements by Schuler and his attorney contrasted with the toxicology report released Tuesday by the Westchester County District Attorney’s Office. In addition to the 0.19 percent blood alcohol level and the presence of marijuana, tests showed that Diane Schuler had 6 grams of alcohol in her stomach that had not yet been metabolized, according to Maj. William Carey of the New York State Police.

Meanwhile, an attorney representing the families of two SUV occupants who died in the wreck said a lawsuit is likely.

“If I could prognosticate, it appears that there will be a civil suit,” said Marshall Nemark, an attorney representing the families of Michael Bastardi and his son, Guy Bastardi, who were killed in the crash along with a friend.

NEW YORK (CNN) — The husband of a woman who, according to authorities, was under the influence of both marijuana and alcohol when she triggered a wrong-way, head-on crash that killed eight people, including herself, has denied allegations that his wife abused substances.

Daniel Schuler appeared at a news conference Thursday with his attorney, Dominic Barbara, to challenge officials’ account of what happened.

“Since the day I met her, I’ve never seen her drunk,” Daniel Schuler said of his wife, Diane. “I’m not angry at her. I’d marry her again tomorrow.”

Schuler’s public remarks came after authorities said Tuesday that 36-year-old Diane Schuler had a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.19 percent — more than twice the legal driving limit — and marijuana in her body when she drove a minivan the wrong way on the Taconic State Parkway and collided head-on with an SUV.

The July 26 crash killed the three adults traveling in the SUV, as well as Diane Schuler and four children in the minivan: her daughter and three nieces. A fifth child in the minivan, Schuler’s son, survived.

At Thursday’s news conference, Barbara pointed to several medical problems he said Diane Schuler had been experiencing before the wreck. He said she apparently had suffered from a tooth abscess for two months, had diabetes at “various levels,” and had a puzzling lump on her leg that appeared to shift location.

“I think she had a stroke,” Barbara said, while acknowledging that he had no proof for that theory. “And I think from the stroke came all the other issues of what happened.”

The collision occurred roughly 30 miles north of New York City after Schuler and the children departed from a campground where her family had been staying. Barbara said no one at the campsite saw Diane Schuler drinking alcohol. He also said investigators had spoken with nine people who interacted with her before she left, and none of them detected the smell of alcohol or marijuana on her breath.

“Actually, it was the opposite,” Barbara said. “She was happy. She was talking to people.”

Authorities said Tuesday that investigators found a broken vodka bottle inside the minivan after the crash. Barbara said he could not account for the bottle, but added, “Something had to have happened.”

Daniel Schuler and his attorney said they had not yet determined whether they would seek a second autopsy.

Jay Schuler, Daniel Schuler’s sister, said Thursday that Diane Schuler was dependable and cared deeply about children.

“There’s no way she’d do this,” Jay Schuler said. “She was responsible.”

The comments from Schuler and his lawyer contrasted with the toxicology findings released Tuesday by the Westchester County District Attorney’s Office. In addition to the 0.19 percent blood-alcohol level and the presence of marijuana, tests found that Diane Schuler had 6 grams of alcohol in her stomach that had not yet been metabolized, according to Maj. William Carey of the New York State Police.

Separately, a lawyer for the families of two of the SUV occupants killed in the crash said a lawsuit is probable.

“If I could prognosticate, it appears that there will be a civil suit,” said Marshall Nemark, who represents the families of Michael Bastardi and his son, Guy Bastardi. Both men died in the crash, along with a friend.

Investigators, however, said the toxicology evidence was significant and that Schuler had consumed alcohol and used marijuana before the crash. Officials also reviewed a series of reported events from earlier that day, including phone calls and witness accounts suggesting she was driving erratically before entering the parkway in the wrong direction.

The crash has left surviving relatives and victims’ families facing potential civil litigation. **BREAKING NEWS: Husband Publicly Defends Wife After Investigators Say Alcohol, Marijuana Led to Deadly Wrong-Way Crash That Killed Eight**

**WESTCHESTER COUNTY, N.Y.** — In an emotional and forceful public defense, Daniel Schuler, the husband of the woman blamed by investigators for one of the deadliest wrong-way crashes in New York history, insisted that his wife was not the intoxicated driver authorities described — even as toxicology results showed she had high levels of alcohol and marijuana in her system.

The crash, which occurred on July 26, 2009, on the Taconic State Parkway, killed eight people, including four children, and stunned the region with its devastating details: a minivan traveling the wrong way for nearly two miles before slamming head-on into an SUV.

At the center of the investigation was **Diane Schuler**, a 36-year-old mother from Long Island, who was driving a red Ford Windstar minivan packed with children returning from a weekend camping trip. She died in the crash, along with her 2-year-old daughter, three young nieces, and three men in the oncoming vehicle.

Authorities later said the evidence was clear: Schuler was severely impaired.

But her husband publicly pushed back.

Daniel Schuler maintained that the findings did not match the woman he knew — a responsible mother, a dependable driver, and someone he said would never knowingly endanger children.

“She was not an alcoholic,” he said in substance during his public defense, rejecting the official portrayal that emerged after investigators released toxicology results. He questioned whether something else — a medical emergency, dental issue, or other unexplained condition — could have caused her erratic behavior before the collision.

Investigators, however, pointed to laboratory results showing Diane Schuler had a blood alcohol content more than twice the legal limit, along with evidence of marijuana use. Authorities said the amount of alcohol in her system was consistent with the equivalent of several drinks and concluded that impairment caused the wrong-way drive and fatal crash.

The case gripped national attention not only because of the number of lives lost, but because of the baffling sequence of events leading up to the crash.

According to investigators and phone records, Schuler had left a campground in Sullivan County that morning with five children in the minivan, including her own son and daughter and three nieces. At some point during the trip, relatives received troubling phone calls suggesting something was wrong. Schuler reportedly sounded disoriented, and one of the children is believed to have said that she was having trouble seeing or speaking clearly.

The minivan later entered the Taconic State Parkway traveling in the wrong direction. Witnesses called 911, describing a vehicle barreling southbound in the northbound lanes. Moments later, the minivan collided head-on with an SUV carrying three men from Yonkers.

All three men in the SUV were killed. Schuler, her daughter, and her three nieces also died. Schuler’s young son survived with serious injuries.

In the aftermath, Daniel Schuler and members of Diane’s family resisted the official explanation. They suggested she may have suffered a sudden medical event, possibly related to an abscessed tooth or other health problem, and they questioned whether the toxicology findings told the whole story.

He also pursued additional review of the case, seeking independent testing and answers that might support an alternative explanation.

But law enforcement officials stood by their conclusions. The medical examiner’s findings and the police investigation attributed the crash to intoxication, saying the evidence did not support the theory that a stroke, heart attack, or other sudden medical emergency caused Schuler to lose control.

The crash remains one of the most discussed impaired-driving tragedies in recent memory — not only because of its scale, but because of the deep divide between the official findings and the family’s insistence that Diane Schuler could not have done what investigators said she did.
